reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey is the closest thing to a measured adoption figure for this sector, and it does not measure nonprofits as a legal category. The series covers Other services, NAICS 81, which includes grantmaking and civic organizations, and asks whether a business used AI in the last two weeks. The latest reading is 15.0%, up from 13.7% in the prior period, with the question first asked in September 2023. That is a proxy, and the Census Bureau suppresses figures where the sample is too thin, so the number describes a broad service-sector bucket rather than the charitable sector on its own.

On what AI is actually used for, the harvested pages establish who studies the question more than what they found. The Center for Effective Philanthropy's sector research, including its AI-focused reporting, examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. NTEN, the Nonprofit Technology Network, runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index is cited here as the citable macro series on AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations. The excerpts themselves are largely organizational homepages, so they name the research programs without reporting their results.

The funding side is where the material gets more concrete. Candid, the nonprofit data organization behind GuideStar and Foundation Center, tracks grantmaking trends including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Its page makes a point that bears on any technology plan: recognition, media coverage, partnerships, and growth do not guarantee a nonprofit's financial sustainability, and organizations need continued unrestricted support to invest. Candid also notes that impact evaluations are becoming more important for both nonprofits and funders, and that giving circles are not a quick fix for lost federal funding. It cites Refuge America, a nonprofit serving LGBTQIA+ asylum seekers and refugees, as an organization hit hard by multiple federal funding cuts.

The access gap gets its own treatment. The AI Equity Project describes building structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs to make AI accessible, ethical, and practical, transforming public libraries and community spaces into learning environments that bring senior citizens and student volunteers together around practical AI tools. It operates as a global network providing standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities, and runs an International AI for Impact Challenge where engineering candidates pitch operational algorithms, with top participants securing lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advisement. NTEN frames the same problem as one of equity, stating that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled, and it promotes an Equity Guide pledge, scholarships for courses and certificates, and open source apps and tools that nonprofit and advocacy groups can put to good use.

The ecosystem catalogue on this site is deliberately narrow and says so. It lists four individually verified organizations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, each classified against a document the organization published about itself. LMSYS is the most directly AI-central entry, stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used to benchmark model quality. Khan Academy is described as an end-user of AI capability in education rather than a producer of it, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software whose missions predate and are not defined by AI. The page states plainly that none of the four are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense, and that the list contains no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights. The notes confirm organizational structure and nonprofit status only, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to governance capacity as the binding constraint, which is how this site frames its own coverage of the sector: grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. The Census Bureau gives a measured baseline, 15.0% against 13.7%, but only for a broader service category. Candid supplies the financial caution about unrestricted support and evaluation burden. NTEN and the AI Equity Project supply the equity and skills framing. What none of these sources provide here is ROI evidence, vendor concentration, or spending figures for nonprofit AI deployment, and the honest reading is that this sector's public evidence base is thinner than its interest in the technology.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: This page catalogues four individually verified organisations ,  two nonprofits and two open-source foundations ,  whose roles touch AI tooling and evaluation, though the page states none are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense. It describes LMSYS as the most directly AI-central entry, stewarding the Chatbot Arena evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, while characterising Khan Academy as an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation are described as stewards of creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, with missions the page says predate and are not defined by AI. The page also flags what its data omits: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights publicly, with the notes confirming only organisational structure and nonprofit status rather than funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
